paragraphs: An objection of a different kind from the one stated and answered in my last address may perhaps also be urged against the principle of legislation for the individual citizens of America. It may be said that this principle would tend to make the government of the Union too powerful, and to enable it to absorb those residual authorities which it might be judged proper to leave with the States for local purposes. I allow the love of power the utmost latitude that any reasonable man could ask, and still I confess I am at a loss to see what temptation the persons entrusted with the administration of the general government could ever feel to strip the States of authorities of that description. The regulation of the mere domestic police of a State seems to me to offer slender allurements to ambition. Commerce, finance, negotiation, and war seem to include all the objects that have charms for minds governed by that passion, and all the powers necessary to those objects ought, in the first instance, to be lodged in the national depository. The administration of private justice between citizens of the same State, the supervision of agriculture and other concerns of a similar nature, all those things, in short, that are proper to be provided for by local legislation, can never be desirable cares for a general jurisdiction. It is therefore improbable that the federal councils would be disposed to usurp the powers with which they are connected, because the attempt to exercise those powers would be as troublesome as it would be useless. For that reason, possessing them would add nothing to the dignity, the importance, or the splendor of the national government.

But let it be granted, for the sake of argument, that mere wantonness and lust of domination would be enough to produce that disposition. Still it may safely be affirmed that the will of the constituent body of the national representatives, in other words the people of the individual States, would restrain the indulgence of so extravagant an appetite. It will always be far easier for the State governments to encroach on the national authorities than for the national government to encroach on the State authorities. The proof of this proposition rests on the greater influence that the State governments will generally have over the people, if they administer their affairs with uprightness and prudence. This circumstance at the same time teaches us that there is an inherent and intrinsic weakness in all federal constitutions, and that too much care cannot be taken in organizing them to give them all the force that is compatible with the principles of liberty.

The superiority of influence in favor of the particular governments would result partly from the diffuse construction of the national government, but chiefly from the nature of the objects to which the State administrations would direct their attention.

It is a known fact of human nature that its affections are commonly weak in proportion to the distance or diffuseness of the object. On the same principle by which a man is more attached to his family than to his neighborhood, and to his neighborhood than to the community at large, the people of each State would tend to feel a stronger bias toward their local governments than toward the government of the Union. This would hold unless a much better administration of the latter destroyed the force of that principle.
This strong propensity of the human heart would find powerful auxiliaries in the objects of State regulation.

The variety of more minute interests which will necessarily fall under the supervision of the local administrations, and which will form so many rivulets of influence running through every part of society, cannot be listed without going into a detail too tedious and uninteresting to repay the instruction it might offer.

There is one transcendent advantage belonging to the province of the State governments which alone suffices to place the matter in a clear and satisfactory light. I mean the ordinary administration of criminal and civil justice. This, of all others, is the most powerful, most universal, and most attractive source of popular obedience and attachment. It is the immediate and visible guardian of life and property. Its benefits and its terrors are in constant activity before the public eye. It regulates all those personal interests and familiar concerns to which the feelings of individuals are most immediately alive. For these reasons it contributes, more than any other circumstance, to impressing on the minds of the people affection, esteem, and reverence toward the government. This great cement of society will spread almost wholly through the channels of the particular governments. Quite apart from all other causes of influence, it would give them so decided a hold over their respective citizens as to make them at all times a complete counterpoise to the power of the Union, and not infrequently dangerous rivals of it.

The operations of the national government, on the other hand, fall less directly under the observation of the mass of the citizens, so the benefits derived from it will chiefly be noticed and attended to by speculative men. Since it concerns more general interests, it will be less apt to come home to the feelings of the people. In the same proportion it will be less likely to inspire a habitual sense of obligation and an active feeling of attachment.
The reasoning on this point has been abundantly borne out by the experience of all the federal constitutions we know of, and of all others that have borne the least resemblance to them.

Though the ancient feudal systems were not, strictly speaking, confederacies, they shared the nature of that kind of association. There was a common head, chieftain, or sovereign, whose authority extended over the whole nation. There were a number of subordinate vassals, or feudatories, who had large portions of land allotted to them, and numerous trains of INFERIOR vassals or retainers who occupied and cultivated that land on the tenure of fealty or obedience to the persons from whom they held it. Each principal vassal was a kind of sovereign within his own particular domains. The consequences of this situation were continual opposition to the authority of the sovereign and frequent wars between the great barons, or chief feudatories, themselves. The power of the head of the nation was commonly too weak either to preserve the public peace or to protect the people against the oppressions of their immediate lords. Historians emphatically call this period of European affairs the times of feudal anarchy.

When the sovereign happened to be a man of vigorous and warlike temper and of superior abilities, he would acquire a personal weight and influence which served, for the time, in place of a more regular authority. But in general the power of the barons triumphed over that of the prince, and in many instances his dominion was entirely thrown off and the great fiefs were set up as independent principalities or States. In those instances in which the monarch finally prevailed over his vassals, his success was chiefly owing to the tyranny of those vassals over their dependents. The barons, or nobles, were equally the enemies of the sovereign and the oppressors of the common people, and were dreaded and detested by both. At length mutual danger and mutual interest brought about a union between the sovereign and the people that was fatal to the power of the aristocracy. Had the nobles, by a conduct of mercy and justice, preserved the fidelity and devotion of their retainers and followers, their contests with the prince must almost always have ended in their favor, and in the reduction or overthrow of the royal authority.

This is not an assertion founded merely on speculation or conjecture. Among other illustrations of its truth that might be cited, Scotland will furnish a compelling example. The spirit of clanship was introduced into that kingdom at an early day, uniting the nobles and their dependents by ties equivalent to those of kindred. It made the aristocracy a constant overmatch for the power of the monarch, until the union with England subdued its fierce and ungovernable spirit and brought it within those rules of subordination which a more rational and more energetic system of civil government had previously established in the latter kingdom.

The separate governments in a confederacy may aptly be compared with the feudal baronies. They have this advantage in their favor: for the reasons already explained, they will generally possess the confidence and good will of the people, and with so important a support they will be able effectively to oppose all encroachments of the national government. It will be well if they are not able to counteract its legitimate and necessary authority. The points of similarity are the rivalry of power that applies to both, and the CONCENTRATION of large portions of the strength of the community in particular DEPOSITORIES, which in one case are at the disposal of individuals and in the other at the disposal of political bodies.

A concise review of the events that have attended confederate governments will further illustrate this important doctrine. Inattention to it has been the great source of our political mistakes and has pointed our jealousy in the wrong direction. This review shall be the subject of some ensuing papers.
